summary: Atypical antipsychotic used for schizophrenia and bipolar depression. Taken once daily with a real meal (≥350 calories) so your body actually absorbs it. Lower metabolic risk than many antipsychotics, but watch for akathisia, parkinsonism, sedation, and rare serious reactions like NMS.
description: Latuda (lurasidone) is a second-generation antipsychotic used to treat schizophrenia and depressive episodes in bipolar I disorder. It can start helping within 1–2 weeks, with more noticeable improvement over 4–6 weeks. The big “gotcha” is absorption: you need to take it with at least 350 calories, or the dose can basically under-deliver. Compared with many antipsychotics, it’s usually more weight- and lipid-friendly, but it can still cause akathisia (inner restlessness), parkinsonism, nausea, and sleep changes. It is not approved for dementia-related psychosis due to increased mortality risk seen with antipsychotics in that population.
patient_summary: Latuda is used for schizophrenia and bipolar depression. Take it once daily with food (≥350 calories) or it may not work as intended. Some people feel less depression or clearer thinking within 1–2 weeks, with fuller benefit by 4–6 weeks. Common issues are restlessness (akathisia), stiffness/shakiness (parkinsonism), nausea, and sleep disruption or sleepiness. Compared with many antipsychotics it tends to be lighter on weight and cholesterol, but metabolic monitoring still matters. It’s not approved for dementia-related psychosis because antipsychotics raise the risk of death in that group.

primary.context: Lurasidone is an FDA-approved option for schizophrenia in adults and adolescents. Improvement may begin within 1–2 weeks, with continued gains through 4–6 weeks.
FDA-approved for depressive episodes in bipolar I disorder as monotherapy and (in adults) as adjunct to lithium or divalproex. Not effective for acute bipolar mania or hypomania.

off_label.context: Sometimes used for depressive episodes with mixed features in bipolar disorder or major depressive disorder. This is off-label and should be specialist-guided.
Used off-label in postpartum psychosis in some protocols with higher-dose titration and a defined treatment window (months), under psychiatric specialty care.

therapeutic_response.display: Schizophrenia: initial effects often within 1–2 weeks; Bipolar depression: initial effects often within 1 week with continued improvement through ~6 weeks

common_adverse_effects.incidence: Adults: ~6% to 22% reported; adolescents also reported
common_adverse_effects.notes: This can feel like anxiety, but it’s more physical—an internal motor that won’t shut off. It often appears early or after dose increases. If you’re pacing, can’t sit through a movie, or feel ‘crawly’ in your body, tell your prescriber quickly—this is treatable and sometimes a reason to slow titration or switch.

common_adverse_effects.incidence: Adults: EPS reported up to ~5% to 39%; parkinsonism ~5% to 17%
common_adverse_effects.notes: Stiffness, tremor, slowed movement, jaw tightness, or swallowing changes can happen. These side effects are dose-related and may show up days to weeks after starting or increasing the dose.

Latuda is often described as mildly to moderately sedating compared with other antipsychotics. Some people feel sleepy at night (helpful), others feel foggy. Sedation often improves over time, but if it’s flattening you, the dose or timing may need adjustment.
Yes, both can happen: some people get sleepy, others get wired. If sleep gets worse, it may be dose-related, timing-related, or actually akathisia masquerading as ‘insomnia.’
Taking it with food helps tolerability and absorption. If nausea shows up early, it often settles, but persistent nausea matters—don’t just suffer through it silently.

common_adverse_effects.incidence: Weight gain reported ~2% to 7%; lipid/glucose changes reported in labeling
common_adverse_effects.notes: Latuda is usually more metabolically friendly than many antipsychotics, and some people even improve labs when switching from higher-risk meds. Still: monitor weight, glucose/A1C, and lipids because risk isn’t zero.

common_adverse_effects.incidence: Dose-dependent; elevated prolactin reported (higher thresholds noted in labeling tables)
common_adverse_effects.notes: If you notice sexual side effects, menstrual changes, breast tenderness or discharge, acne/hirsutism changes, or fertility issues, bring it up. Sometimes the fix is dose, switching, or choosing a more prolactin-sparing option.

serious_risks.risk: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): fever, severe rigidity, confusion, autonomic instability. MEDICAL EMERGENCY.
Tardive dyskinesia: involuntary movements (face/tongue/limbs), risk increases with long-term exposure and age; can be persistent.
Severe orthostatic hypotension/syncope and falls: injury risk, especially in older adults or dehydration.
Hematologic abnormalities: leukopenia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia—monitor CBC if history of low counts or symptoms of infection.
Hyperglycemia/diabetes: uncommon compared with some SGAs but possible; monitor labs and symptoms (thirst, urination, fatigue).

Cardiac conduction issues/QT prolongation: overall QTc effect is minimal compared with many antipsychotics, but postmarketing QT prolongation has been reported—use caution with cardiac risk factors or interacting meds.
Temperature dysregulation/heat stroke risk: especially during heat exposure, dehydration, strenuous exercise.
Suicidal ideation reported postmarketing: monitor mood and safety, especially during early treatment or changes.

safety.black_box_warning: Elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotic drugs are at an increased risk of death. Lurasidone is not approved for the treatment of patients with dementia-related psychosis.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Adherence and dosing-with-food check at every visit: confirm ≥350 calories each dose and consistent timing
Mental status and target symptoms every visit: mood, psychosis intensity, agitation, sleep, functioning

Akathisia/EPS every visit (and ~4 weeks after initiation or dose change): ask directly about restlessness and do a brief movement exam; use a formal rating scale at least annually (more often if high risk)
Tardive dyskinesia screening every visit and formally at least annually (every 6 months if high risk): look for subtle face/tongue/hand movements early
Fall risk and orthostatic vitals every visit early on and after dose changes; counsel on slow position changes
Weight/BMI at baseline, around 8 and 12 weeks after start or dose change, then quarterly; consider waist circumference at baseline and annually
Fasting plasma glucose/A1C around 4 months after initiation, then annually (more often if abnormal or high risk)
Lipid panel around 4 months after initiation, then annually (more often if abnormal or high risk)

special_populations.pregnancy: Class-level data for second-generation antipsychotics do not show a clear major increase in congenital malformations overall, but lurasidone-specific data are limited. Third-trimester exposure to antipsychotics can lead to newborn EPS and/or withdrawal symptoms (agitation, abnormal tone, feeding issues, respiratory distress, somnolence, tremor). Avoiding relapse is often the priority—stopping an effective medication can raise relapse risk. Use the lowest effective dose and avoid polytherapy when possible; monitor symptom severity with a validated tool throughout pregnancy.
special_populations.lactation: Lurasidone is present in human milk. Limited data from one lactating patient suggest low infant exposure (relative infant dose reported <1%) and no observed adverse events in that case, but evidence is thin. If breastfeeding during treatment, monitor the infant for sedation, poor feeding, irritability, motor abnormalities, and slowed development—especially if the infant is premature/low birth weight or if other sedating medications are involved. Use the lowest effective dose and avoid multiple sedating meds when possible.
special_populations.pediatric: Bipolar depression: approved down to age 10 (monotherapy). Schizophrenia: approved in adolescents. Pediatric patients may have higher EPS risk and require careful metabolic monitoring (weight/BMI, glucose/A1C, lipids) and movement monitoring. Long-term usefulness should be periodically reevaluated as part of a total treatment plan (therapy, school supports, family work).
special_populations.geriatric: Avoid antipsychotics for behavioral problems associated with dementia or delirium unless nonpharmacologic therapies fail and the patient is at risk of harming self or others. Antipsychotics increase mortality risk in dementia-related psychosis. If used for appropriate indications (eg, schizophrenia or bipolar disorder), use the lower range of adult dosing, titrate slowly, and monitor orthostasis, falls, movement symptoms, cognition, and sodium.
special_populations.renal_impairment: CrCl <50 mL/min: start 20 mg daily; max 80 mg/day. CrCl ≥50 mL/min: no adjustment.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Moderate hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B): start 20 mg daily; max 80 mg/day. Severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C): start 20 mg daily; max 40 mg/day.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Increased in fed state; taking with ≥350 calories increases exposure substantially compared with fasting
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Primarily hepatic via CYP3A4; has active and inactive metabolites
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Requires food (≥350 calories) for reliable absorption; grapefruit may increase serum concentrations

dosing.titration: Latuda is typically taken once daily in the evening with food (at least 350 calories). The food requirement is not optional—without it, absorption drops hard. Dosing depends on the psychiatric indication and special factors like kidney/liver function and age.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: With chronic psychiatric illness, switching is often safer than “just stopping,” especially if Latuda is controlling psychosis or bipolar depression. If stopping is the plan, taper gradually over weeks to months so you can catch early relapse signals and reduce withdrawal reactions (agitation, anxiety, insomnia, sweating, GI upset, tremor, dyskinesias). If discontinuation is due to a serious adverse effect, the plan may need to be faster—this is where specialist guidance matters.

sections.intro: Everyone’s response is personal, but here’s what tends to show up in real life—especially in the first few weeks:

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Latuda isn’t an instant tranquilizer. It’s more of a steady-build medication—early changes first, then deeper improvement over weeks.
key_points: Within 1 week (often): early improvement in bipolar depression can start showing up
1–2 weeks: early schizophrenia symptom shifts may begin (less intensity, less agitation)
4–6 weeks: fuller effect is more likely to be noticeable and consistent
Once daily dosing: long half-life supports daily dosing rather than multiple times per day
Food is part of the dose: taking it with ≥350 calories meaningfully changes how much medication your body absorbs

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Latuda can be effective for bipolar depression and schizophrenia, but it typically works in layers: early shifts in the first 1–2 weeks, followed by steadier improvement over 4–6 weeks. Consistency matters—and with this medication, the food requirement is part of consistency.
sections.clinical_details: In practice, response is strongly tied to (1) taking it with sufficient food and (2) tolerability during titration, especially around akathisia and parkinsonism. If someone ‘fails’ Latuda while taking it fasting, that may not be a real trial. If someone can’t tolerate akathisia, efficacy becomes irrelevant—management and switching strategies matter.

sections.intro: Latuda is primarily metabolized by CYP3A4. Strong inhibitors can raise levels dangerously, and strong inducers can make it stop working. This is one of the most important interaction profiles to respect.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: With chronic psychiatric illness, switching is often safer than “just stopping,” especially if Latuda is controlling psychosis or bipolar depression. If stopping is the plan, taper gradually over weeks to months so you can catch early relapse signals and reduce withdrawal reactions (agitation, anxiety, insomnia, sweating, GI upset, tremor, dyskinesias). If discontinuation is due to a serious adverse effect, the plan may need to be faster—this is where specialist guidance matters.
key_points: Don’t stop abruptly unless there’s a serious adverse effect requiring urgent discontinuation.
Taper over several weeks to months when possible to reduce withdrawal symptoms and detect symptom recurrence early.

Withdrawal symptoms can include agitation, anxiety, insomnia, sweating, GI symptoms, chills/warmth waves, tremor, restlessness, dizziness/vertigo, dyskinesias, and return of psychosis or mood symptoms.

If switching antipsychotics: common strategies include cross-titration, overlap-and-taper, or (less commonly) abrupt change with careful monitoring; relapse risk level should drive how conservative you are.
If schizophrenia relapse risk is high, clinicians may overlap (keep the current med stable while the new med reaches a therapeutic dose) before tapering the first medication.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Latuda is typically taken once daily in the evening with food (at least 350 calories). The food requirement is not optional—without it, absorption drops hard. Dosing depends on the psychiatric indication and special factors like kidney/liver function and age.

adult.schizophrenia_initial: 40 mg PO once daily in the evening within 30 minutes of food (≥350 calories); consider 20 mg once daily for first-episode psychosis or sensitivity to side effects
adult.schizophrenia_titration: Increase in 40 mg increments no sooner than every 3 days based on response and tolerability; monitor akathisia, parkinsonism, and sedation during titration
adult.schizophrenia_typical: 40 to 80 mg/day; use the lowest effective maintenance dose
adult.bipolar_depression_initial: 20 mg PO once daily in the evening within 30 minutes of food (≥350 calories)
adult.bipolar_depression_titration: Increase by 20 mg increments every ≥2 days based on response and tolerability
adult.mdd_mixed_features_initial: 20 mg PO once daily in the evening within 30 minutes of food (≥350 calories) for 7 days
adult.mdd_mixed_features_titration: After day 7, increase by 20 mg every 2 to 7 days based on response and tolerability
adult.postpartum_psychosis_initial: 40 mg PO once daily in the evening within 30 minutes of food (≥350 calories)
adult.postpartum_psychosis_titration: After 3 days increase to 80 mg once daily; after 2 to 3 additional days may increase further up to 160 mg/day over ~1 week based on response and tolerability
adult.renal_impairment: CrCl <50 mL/min: Start 20 mg PO daily; maximum 80 mg/day (CrCl ≥50 mL/min: no adjustment)
adult.hepatic_impairment: Child-Pugh B: Start 20 mg PO daily; maximum 80 mg/day. Child-Pugh C: Start 20 mg PO daily; maximum 40 mg/day (Child-Pugh A: no adjustment)
adult.older_adults: Use lower-end adult doses and titrate slowly; avoid for dementia-related behavioral symptoms unless nonpharmacologic strategies fail and there is risk of harm; monitor falls, orthostasis, sodium, and movement symptoms closely

sections.simple_explanation: Latuda is usually once daily. The single most important dosing rule is food: take it with at least 350 calories or you won’t absorb enough. Dose increases should be slow enough to catch akathisia, stiffness, sedation, or blood pressure drops early. Kidney and liver impairment lower your safe maximum dose.

For kids and teens, metabolic and movement monitoring matters even if a medication is considered “lower risk.”

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Latuda is an oral tablet. Generics are available in the same strengths. Tablets should be taken with food and are generally not recommended to be split, crushed, or cut (the effects of altering tablets haven’t been fully evaluated).
items: Tablets: 20 mg, 40 mg, 60 mg, 80 mg, 120 mg (brand and generic availability varies by country)
Administration: Once daily with food (≥350 calories), ideally at the same time each day

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Latuda works by balancing dopamine and serotonin signaling in the brain—mainly by blocking dopamine D2 receptors and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors, with additional activity at 5-HT7 and partial agonism at 5-HT1A. The dopamine piece targets psychosis and agitation; the serotonin profile may help mood and cognition. It has little to no meaningful activity at histamine H1 or muscarinic M1 receptors, which is one reason it’s often less sedating and less anticholinergic than some alternatives—though side effects can still happen.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Latuda is a common choice when treating schizophrenia or bipolar depression, especially if weight gain, diabetes risk, or lipid issues are a major concern with other antipsychotics. It’s not a medication for acute mania/hypomania. The biggest practical rule is absorption: you need a real meal (≥350 calories). If you don’t build that into your routine, you can end up with inconsistent benefit and confusing side effects. Titration should be guided by tolerability—akathisia and parkinsonism are the side effects that most often determine whether Latuda is the right fit.

faqs.a: Latuda (lurasidone) is used to treat schizophrenia and depressive episodes in bipolar I disorder (bipolar depression). It’s not a treatment for acute bipolar mania or hypomania.

Some people notice early changes within about 1–2 weeks (sometimes sooner for bipolar depression), but the more consistent benefit usually builds over 4–6 weeks. If you’re not taking it with enough food, it can look like it “isn’t working” even when the dose is right on paper.

faqs.q: Do I really have to take Latuda with food?
faqs.a: Yes. Latuda needs at least 350 calories to absorb properly. Without food, your body gets way less of the medication—so you can end up with inconsistent results and a very confusing trial.

faqs.q: What’s the most common reason people stop Latuda?
faqs.a: Akathisia (that intense internal restlessness) is a big one. It can feel like anxiety but it’s more physical—pacing, can’t sit still, “crawling” energy. The good news: it’s often manageable if caught early, and sometimes it means slowing the titration or choosing a different medication.

Compared with many antipsychotics, Latuda is usually associated with minimal to low weight and metabolic risk. But “lower risk” doesn’t mean “no risk.” Some people still gain weight or have changes in glucose or lipids, so monitoring matters.

faqs.q: What medications can’t be taken with Latuda?
faqs.a: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors and strong CYP3A4 inducers are the major problem and are generally contraindicated (they can make levels dangerously high or make the medication ineffective). Grapefruit can also raise levels—avoid it.

faqs.q: Is Latuda approved for dementia-related psychosis?
faqs.a: No. Antipsychotics increase mortality risk in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis, and Latuda is not approved for that use.

faqs.q: How do I stop Latuda safely?
faqs.a: Don’t stop abruptly unless there’s a serious adverse effect that requires urgent discontinuation. If stopping is the plan, taper gradually over weeks to months so you can catch early relapse symptoms and reduce withdrawal reactions like agitation, anxiety, insomnia, sweating, tremor, GI upset, and return of psychosis or mood symptoms.

Latuda has been used off-label in postpartum psychosis in some specialist-guided protocols. Postpartum decisions are high-stakes—treatment should be individualized, and risks of untreated illness are real. If breastfeeding, infant monitoring for sedation/feeding issues is important because lurasidone can be present in milk.

faqs.q: What should be monitored while taking Latuda?
faqs.a: At visits: symptoms, side effects, movement symptoms (akathisia/EPS/TD), orthostatic vitals/fall risk, and adherence—including the food requirement. Over time: weight/BMI, glucose/A1C, lipids, and prolactin symptoms. CBC and chemistries are checked as clinically indicated, especially if there’s a history of low white blood cells or other risk factors.
